intro: A practical reference to English grammar for learners. Each group explains one area with short rules, clear patterns, examples and tables. Use it to check a form quickly or to revise a topic in order.

groups.title: Grammar basics
groups.summary: How sentences are built, how subjects and verbs agree, and how to form questions, negatives and instructions.

sections.title: Sentence patterns
sections.intro: Every English sentence needs a subject and a verb. The verb decides whether an object or a complement is also needed.

rules.title: Core sentence patterns
rules.pattern: S + V / S + V + O / S + V + C
rules.explanation: An intransitive verb needs only a subject. A transitive verb needs an object. A linking verb joins the subject to a complement that describes it. Some verbs also take two objects: a person and a thing.

examples.text: Birds fly.
She reads novels.
He is a teacher.
Mum gave me a lift.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She reads. (when you mean she reads something) Right: She reads novels.

rows: Only a subject and a verb

sections.title: Agreement and word order
sections.intro: The verb must match its subject, and English normally puts information in a fixed order.

rules.title: Subject-verb agreement
rules.pattern: singular subject + singular verb; plural subject + plural verb
rules.explanation: In the present simple, add -s to the verb with he, she and it. Use the base form with I, you, we and they. The verb agrees with its subject, not with a phrase that follows it.

examples.text: She works in a bank.
They work from home.
The list of names is long.
examples.note: The subject is list, not names.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The list of names are long. Right: The list of names is long.

rules.title: Basic word order
rules.pattern: S + V + O + manner + place + time
rules.explanation: English normally puts the subject before the verb and the object after it. Adverbials usually follow in the order manner, place, time, but a time expression can also come first for emphasis.

examples.text: She sang the song beautifully at the concert last night.
We walked slowly to the station this morning.
Yesterday we stayed at home.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I like very much this film. Right: I like this film very much.

rows: who or what does the action
who or what receives the action

sections.title: Questions and negatives
sections.intro: Most questions and negatives need an auxiliary verb. If there is no auxiliary, use do, does or did.

rules.title: Questions
rules.pattern: Auxiliary + subject + main verb? / Question word + auxiliary + subject + main verb?
rules.explanation: Most questions put an auxiliary before the subject. If there is no auxiliary, add do, does or did and use the base form of the main verb. When the question word is the subject, do not add an auxiliary.

examples.text: Are you ready?
Where do you work?
Who called you?

rules.mistake: Wrong: Where you are going? Right: Where are you going?

rules.title: Negatives
rules.explanation: Put not after the first auxiliary. If there is no auxiliary, use do not, does not or did not plus the base verb.

examples.text: I do not like coffee.
She is not coming.
They have not finished.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I not like coffee. Right: I do not like coffee.

sections.title: There is, there are and imperatives
sections.intro: Use there is and there are to say that something exists. Use the imperative to give instructions and warnings.

rules.title: There is and there are
rules.pattern: There is + singular or uncountable noun; There are + plural noun
rules.explanation: Use there is before a singular or uncountable noun and there are before a plural noun. The verb agrees with the noun that follows it.

examples.text: There is a bank near here.
There are two chairs in the room.
There is some milk in the fridge.

rules.mistake: Wrong: There have a bank near here. Right: There is a bank near here.

rules.title: Imperatives
rules.pattern: Base verb (+ object) / Do not + base verb
rules.explanation: Use the base verb to give an instruction, direction or warning. Add please to be polite, and use do not or don't for a negative instruction.

examples.text: Close the door, please.
Turn left at the lights.
Do not touch the wires.

rules.mistake: Wrong: You close the door. (as a command) Right: Close the door.

groups.title: Nouns
groups.summary: Countability, plurals, possessives, articles, quantifiers and pronouns.

sections.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
sections.intro: Nouns are countable when you can count them one by one. Uncountable nouns name things that are not counted in units.

rules.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
rules.pattern: countable: a/an + singular, plural forms; uncountable: no a/an, singular verb
rules.explanation: Countable nouns can be counted and have singular and plural forms. Uncountable nouns do not normally have a plural and do not take a/an; they take a singular verb.

examples.text: I bought a book and two magazines.
She gave me some advice.
Water boils at 100 degrees.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She gave me an advice. Right: She gave me some advice.

rules.title: Nouns that can be both
rules.pattern: uncountable general meaning / countable type or portion
rules.explanation: Some nouns are uncountable in a general sense but countable when they mean a type, a portion or a particular example.

examples.text: I like coffee.
Two coffees, please.
The region produces excellent wines.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I need a paper to write on. (meaning material) Right: I need some paper to write on.

rows: The window is made of glass.

sections.title: Plurals and possessives
sections.intro: Most plurals are regular, but some are irregular. Possessives show who owns or is connected to something.

rules.title: Plurals
rules.explanation: Add -s to most nouns and -es after -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x or -z. Change consonant + y to -ies. Some plurals are irregular and must be learned.

examples.text: books, boxes, cities
man -> men, child -> children
sheep -> sheep, fish -> fish

rules.mistake: Wrong: three childs. Right: three children.

rules.title: Possessives
rules.explanation: Add 's to a singular noun and to an irregular plural. Add only an apostrophe to a regular plural ending in -s. Use of for things, ideas and quantities.

examples.text: the teacher's desk
the students' books
the children's toys
the end of the film

rules.mistake: Wrong: the childrens' toys. Right: the children's toys.

sections.title: Articles and quantifiers
sections.intro: Articles show whether a noun is general or specific. Quantifiers show how much or how many.

rules.title: A, an, the and zero article
rules.pattern: a/an + singular countable; the + known or unique; no article for general plurals and uncountables
rules.explanation: Use a/an for one of many or a first mention. Use the when the listener can identify the thing, when it is unique, or when it was mentioned before. Use no article for general plurals, uncountables and most names.

examples.text: I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.
The sun is bright today.
Cats are independent.
She speaks French.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The life is difficult. Right: Life is difficult.

rules.title: Quantifiers
rules.pattern: some/any + plural or uncountable; much/many; a few/a little
rules.explanation: Use some in positive sentences and any in negatives and most questions. Use many and a few with countable plurals, and much and a little with uncountables.

examples.text: I have some money.
We do not have any milk.
How many books do you have?
There is a little milk left.

rules.mistake: Wrong: How much students are there? Right: How many students are there?

rows: a few coins, a little salt

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.intro: Pronouns replace nouns so that you do not have to repeat them. Their form changes according to their job in the sentence.

rules.title: Personal, possessive and reflexive pronouns
rules.pattern: subject: I, you, he, she, it, we, they; object: me, you, him, her, it, us, them
rules.explanation: Use a subject pronoun before the verb and an object pronoun after a verb or preposition. Possessive adjectives come before a noun; possessive pronouns stand alone. Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject when the subject and object are the same.

examples.text: She called him.
This is my bag. It is mine.
She taught herself to swim.
Someone left their bag.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Me and Tom went out. Right: Tom and I went out.

groups.title: Verbs
groups.summary: Verb forms, auxiliaries, gerunds and infinitives, stative verbs and phrasal verbs.

sections.title: Verb forms and auxiliaries
sections.intro: Verbs change form for tense and person. Auxiliary verbs help the main verb form questions, negatives and complex tenses.

rules.title: Verb forms and irregular verbs
rules.explanation: Most verbs have five forms. Regular verbs add -ed for the past and past participle. Irregular verbs change in other ways and must be learned.

examples.text: work, works, worked, worked, working
write, writes, wrote, written, writing
put, puts, put, put, putting

rules.mistake: Wrong: I have went. Right: I have gone.

rules.title: Auxiliary verbs and do-support
rules.explanation: Be forms continuous tenses and the passive. Do forms questions and negatives in the simple present and past. Have forms perfect tenses. After do, does or did, the main verb stays in the base form.

examples.text: She is reading.
Do you know him?
They have left.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Did she went home? Right: Did she go home?

sections.title: Gerunds and infinitives
sections.intro: Some verbs are followed by the -ing form, others by to + base verb, and a few by the base verb alone.

rules.title: Gerunds after verbs
rules.explanation: Some verbs are followed by a gerund, especially verbs of liking, disliking, finishing and suggesting. A gerund can also be the subject of a sentence.

examples.text: I enjoy reading.
She suggested going by train.
Swimming is good exercise.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I enjoy to read. Right: I enjoy reading.

rules.title: Infinitives and bare verbs
rules.pattern: verb + to + base verb; modal/let/make + base verb
rules.explanation: Some verbs are followed by a to-infinitive. After modal auxiliaries and after let, make, see and hear in the active, use the base verb without to. A few verbs change meaning with -ing or to.

examples.text: I want to leave.
You must go.
I stopped smoking last year.
I stopped to buy milk.

rules.mistake: Wrong: You must to go. Right: You must go.

sections.title: Stative and phrasal verbs
sections.intro: Stative verbs describe states rather than actions. Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle to make a new meaning.

rules.title: Stative verbs
rules.explanation: Stative verbs describe states, thoughts, feelings, possession or senses. They are not normally used in continuous tenses. Some can be dynamic with a different meaning.

examples.text: I know the answer.
She owns two cars.
I am thinking about you.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I am knowing the answer. Right: I know the answer.

rules.title: Phrasal verbs
rules.explanation: The meaning of a phrasal verb is often different from the verb alone. With separable phrasal verbs, the object can go between the verb and particle. With inseparable ones, it must come after the particle.

examples.text: I woke up at seven.
Turn off the light. / Turn the light off.
I look after my sister.
She ran into an old friend.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Turn off it. Right: Turn it off.

rows: I put up with the noise.

groups.title: Tenses
groups.summary: The twelve English tenses and the main ways of talking about the future.

sections.title: Present tenses
sections.intro: The present tenses cover habits, current actions and connections between the past and now.

rules.title: Present simple
rules.explanation: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts and permanent situations. It is common with always, usually, often, sometimes and never.

examples.text: She works in a hospital.
Water boils at 100 degrees.
I do not eat meat.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She work in a hospital. Right: She works in a hospital.

rules.title: Present continuous
rules.explanation: Use the present continuous for actions happening now, temporary situations and fixed arrangements in the near future.

examples.text: I am writing an email.
They are staying with us this week.
We are meeting Anna tomorrow.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I am knowing the answer. Right: I know the answer.

rules.title: Present perfect
rules.explanation: Use the present perfect for past actions with a connection to now, for experiences without a specific time, and for situations that started in the past and continue.

examples.text: I have lost my keys.
She has visited Japan twice.
We have lived here since 2020.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I have seen him yesterday. Right: I saw him yesterday.

rules.title: Present perfect continuous
rules.explanation: Use the present perfect continuous for an action that started in the past and is still continuing, or has just stopped and has a visible result. It often answers 'how long?'.

examples.text: I have been studying for three hours.
She has been running, so she is tired.
How long have you been waiting?

rules.mistake: Wrong: I am studying here for three hours. Right: I have been studying here for three hours.

rows: past with a link to now

sections.title: Past tenses
sections.intro: The past tenses place actions at a past time and show how past actions relate to each other.

rules.title: Past simple
rules.explanation: Use the past simple for completed actions at a definite time in the past, and for a sequence of past events.

examples.text: I saw her yesterday.
They moved to Leeds in 2019.
She opened the door and walked in.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I have seen her yesterday. Right: I saw her yesterday.

rules.title: Past continuous
rules.explanation: Use the past continuous for an action in progress at a particular time in the past, often interrupted by another action.

examples.text: I was cooking when you called.
They were watching TV at eight.
It was raining all morning.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I was cook when you called. Right: I was cooking when you called.

rules.title: Past perfect
rules.explanation: Use the past perfect for an action completed before another past action or time. It makes the order of past events clear.

examples.text: The film had started when we arrived.
She had never seen the sea before that day.
He had finished before noon.

rules.mistake: Wrong: When we arrived, the film started. (if it started earlier) Right: When we arrived, the film had started.

rules.title: Past perfect continuous
rules.explanation: Use the past perfect continuous for an action that had been happening for some time before another past action or time.

examples.text: She had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
They had been living there for years before they moved.
I had been working all day, so I was tired.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She had been wait for an hour. Right: She had been waiting for an hour.

rows: completed action at a past time
action in progress in the past
duration up to a past point

sections.title: Future tenses
sections.intro: The future tenses use will to show actions at, in progress at, or completed before a future time.

rules.title: Future simple
rules.explanation: Use will for predictions, spontaneous decisions, promises and offers. It does not usually show a plan made before speaking.

examples.text: I will call you later.
It will probably rain tomorrow.
I will help you with that.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I will call you when I will arrive. Right: I will call you when I arrive.

rules.title: Future continuous
rules.explanation: Use the future continuous for an action that will be in progress at a particular time in the future.

examples.text: At eight, I will be travelling to work.
This time tomorrow, we will be lying on the beach.
I will be seeing her at the meeting.

rules.mistake: Wrong: At eight, I will be travel to work. Right: At eight, I will be travelling to work.

rules.title: Future perfect
rules.explanation: Use the future perfect for an action that will be completed before a particular time in the future.

examples.text: By Friday, I will have finished the report.
She will have left by the time we arrive.
In ten years, he will have paid off the loan.

rules.mistake: Wrong: By Friday, I will have finish the report. Right: By Friday, I will have finished the report.

rules.title: Future perfect continuous
rules.explanation: Use the future perfect continuous for an action that will have been continuing for a period up to a particular future time. It emphasises duration.

examples.text: By June, I will have been working here for five years.
Next month, they will have been living together for a year.
At noon, he will have been driving for six hours.

rules.mistake: Wrong: By June, I will have been work here for five years. Right: By June, I will have been working here for five years.

rows: in progress at a future time
duration up to a future time

sections.title: Future forms
sections.intro: English uses several forms for the future. The choice depends on whether you are predicting, planning or following a timetable.

rules.title: Will
rules.explanation: Use will for predictions, instant decisions, promises and offers. Do not use will in a future time clause after when, if, before, after or until.

examples.text: I will open the window.
I promise I will be careful.
When I arrive, I will call you.

rules.mistake: Wrong: When I will arrive, I will call you. Right: When I arrive, I will call you.

rules.title: Going to
rules.explanation: Use going to for plans and intentions decided before speaking, and for predictions based on present evidence.

examples.text: We are going to move house next year.
Look at those clouds - it is going to rain.
She is going to study medicine.

rules.mistake: Wrong: We are go to move house. Right: We are going to move house.

rules.title: Present continuous for future
rules.explanation: Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements in the near future, especially when the time and place are decided.

examples.text: I am meeting Sam at six.
They are flying to Rome on Friday.
We are having dinner with my parents tonight.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I meet Sam at six tomorrow. (fixed arrangement) Right: I am meeting Sam at six tomorrow.

rules.title: Present simple for timetables
rules.explanation: Use the present simple for timetables and schedules, even about the future. This includes transport, films, classes and events.

examples.text: The train leaves at 7:15.
The film starts at eight.
My course begins on Monday.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The train is leave at 7:15. Right: The train leaves at 7:15.

rows: I am meeting Sam at six.

sections.title: The twelve tenses at a glance
sections.intro: Tense combines time (present, past, future) with aspect (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).

rules.title: Choosing a tense
rules.explanation: Choose the time first, then choose the aspect that matches how the action relates to that time. The table below summarises all twelve forms.

examples.text: I work here.
I have worked here since 2020.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I am work here. Right: I work here.

groups.title: Modal verbs
groups.summary: Ability, possibility, obligation, advice, requests and past deduction.

sections.title: Ability, possibility and deduction
sections.intro: Modal verbs add meaning such as ability, possibility or certainty. They are followed by the base verb.

rules.title: Can and could
rules.explanation: Use can for present ability and could for past ability. Could also makes a less direct possibility or a polite request. For other tenses, use be able to.

examples.text: She can swim.
I could read when I was four.
It could rain later.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I can to swim. Right: I can swim.

rules.title: May and might
rules.explanation: Use may and might to say something is possible. Might often suggests a weaker possibility, and may is more formal. For past possibility, use may/might + have + past participle.

examples.text: It may snow tonight.
She might not come.
There may be a delay.

rules.mistake: Wrong: It may rains tonight. Right: It may rain tonight.

rules.title: Deduction and probability
rules.explanation: Use must when you are almost certain something is true and can't when you are almost certain it is not true. May, might and could show different degrees of possibility.

examples.text: You must be tired after that journey.
That can't be true.
This could be the answer.

rules.mistake: Wrong: He can't be at home; his car is here. Right: He must be at home; his car is here.

sections.title: Obligation, necessity and advice
sections.intro: These modals show how strong an obligation is and whether something is necessary, forbidden or simply advisable.

rules.title: Must and have to
rules.explanation: Use must for strong obligation, often from the speaker, and have to for obligation from rules, circumstances or another person. Must has no past form; use had to.

examples.text: You must wear a seat belt.
I have to finish this report by Friday.
We had to leave early.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I musted go. Right: I had to go.

rules.title: Mustn't and don't have to
rules.pattern: must not + verb; do not have to + verb
rules.explanation: Must not (mustn't) means something is forbidden. Do not have to (don't have to) means something is not necessary. The difference is important.

examples.text: You mustn't smoke here.
You don't have to come if you are busy.
We didn't have to pay.

rules.mistake: Wrong: You don't have to smoke here. (if it is forbidden) Right: You mustn't smoke here.

rules.title: Should and ought to
rules.explanation: Use should and ought to for advice, recommendations and what is right. Should is more common; ought to is slightly more formal. For past advice, use should have + past participle.

examples.text: You should see a doctor.
We ought to leave soon.
You shouldn't eat so much sugar.

rules.mistake: Wrong: You should to rest. Right: You should rest.

rules.title: Need and needn't
rules.pattern: need to + base verb; needn't + base verb
rules.explanation: Use need to for necessity. Needn't (need not) means something is not necessary. As a modal, needn't is followed by the base verb.

examples.text: I need to buy milk.
You needn't worry.
She needn't come tomorrow.

rules.mistake: Wrong: You needn't to worry. Right: You needn't worry.

rows: I have to wear a uniform.

sections.title: Requests, offers and willingness
sections.intro: Modal verbs make requests and offers more or less direct and polite.

rules.title: Will, would and shall
rules.explanation: Use will for willingness, offers and promises. Would is more polite for requests and describes past habits. Use shall in offers and suggestions with I and we, especially in British English.

examples.text: I will carry that for you.
Would you close the door, please?
When I was young, we would spend summers by the sea.
Shall I open the window?

rules.mistake: Wrong: Would you to help me? Right: Would you help me?

rules.title: Permission and polite requests
rules.explanation: Can is the usual form for permission; could and may are more polite or formal. For requests, could and would are common.

examples.text: Can I use your phone?
Could I ask a question?
May I come in?

rules.mistake: Wrong: May you help me? (request) Right: Could you help me?

sections.title: Past modals
sections.intro: Modal + have + past participle allows you to make deductions, express regret and criticise past actions.

rules.title: Modal + have + past participle
rules.explanation: Use this structure to talk about the past. Must have = certain; might have = possible; should have = regret or criticism; could have = unrealised possibility; needn't have = did something unnecessary.

examples.text: She must have missed the train.
You should have told me.
I could have won.
You needn't have waited.

rules.mistake: Wrong: You should have tell me. Right: You should have told me.

groups.title: Conditionals
groups.summary: Zero, first, second, third and mixed conditionals, plus unless, wish and if only.

sections.title: Conditional sentences
sections.intro: Conditional sentences describe a condition and its result. The form changes according to whether the situation is real, unreal or impossible.

rules.title: Zero conditional
rules.explanation: Use the zero conditional for general truths, facts and habits. Both clauses use the present simple.

examples.text: If you heat ice, it melts.
If I drink coffee late, I cannot sleep.
Plants die if they get no water.

rules.mistake: Wrong: If you will heat ice, it melts. Right: If you heat ice, it melts.

rules.title: First conditional
rules.pattern: If + present simple, will + base verb
rules.explanation: Use the first conditional for a real or likely future condition and its result. Do not use will in the if-clause.

examples.text: If it rains, we will stay at home.
If you study, you will pass.
I will call you if I arrive early.

rules.mistake: Wrong: If it will rain, we will stay at home. Right: If it rains, we will stay at home.

rules.title: Second conditional
rules.pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb
rules.explanation: Use the second conditional for an unreal or unlikely present or future situation, and for imaginary situations. Use were with I and he/she/it in formal English.

examples.text: If I had more time, I would travel.
If I were you, I would apologise.
What would you do if you lost your phone?

rules.mistake: Wrong: If I would have time, I would travel. Right: If I had time, I would travel.

rules.title: Third conditional
rules.pattern: If + past perfect, would have + past participle
rules.explanation: Use the third conditional for an unreal past situation and its imagined result. It describes something that did not happen.

examples.text: If I had studied, I would have passed.
If we had left earlier, we would not have missed the train.
She would have come if you had invited her.

rules.mistake: Wrong: If I would have studied, I would have passed. Right: If I had studied, I would have passed.

rules.title: Mixed conditionals
rules.pattern: If + past perfect, would + base verb / If + past simple, would have + past participle
rules.explanation: Mixed conditionals combine different times. Use them when the condition is in the past but the result is in the present, or the condition is present and the result is in the past.

examples.text: If I had taken the job, I would be in London now.
If I were more organised, I would have finished yesterday.
If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor now.

rules.mistake: Wrong: If I would have taken the job, I would be in London now. Right: If I had taken the job, I would be in London now.

rows: would + base or would have + past participle

sections.title: Unless, wish and if only
sections.intro: Unless replaces if not. Wish and if only express regrets and desires.

rules.title: Unless
rules.explanation: Unless means 'if not'. Use it to introduce the only condition that would change the result. Do not use not after unless in the same clause.

examples.text: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
I will go unless it rains.
Unless she calls, we will start without her.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Unless you don't hurry, you will miss the bus. Right: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.

rules.title: Wish and if only
rules.pattern: wish/if only + past simple / past perfect / would
rules.explanation: Use the past simple for a present wish, the past perfect for a past regret, and would for a wish about someone else's behaviour. If only is stronger and more emotional than wish.

examples.text: I wish I had more time.
I wish I had studied harder.
If only she would listen.
I wish it would stop raining.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I wish I have more time. Right: I wish I had more time.

groups.title: The passive
groups.summary: Passive forms by tense, when to use the passive, the by-agent, the get-passive and common mistakes.

sections.title: Passive forms
sections.intro: The passive changes the focus from the doer to the action or the receiver. It is formed with be + past participle.

rules.title: Forming the passive
rules.explanation: The object of an active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence. The form of be changes with the tense, but the past participle stays the same.

examples.text: Someone stole my bike. -> My bike was stolen.
They clean the office every day. -> The office is cleaned every day.
The teacher marked the essays. -> The essays were marked by the teacher.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The letter was wrote. Right: The letter was written.

rules.title: Perfect, continuous, future and modal passives
rules.pattern: have/has been + past participle; is being + past participle; will be + past participle; modal + be + past participle
rules.explanation: The passive can be used in most tenses and with modals. Continuous passives use being. Only verbs that take an object can normally be made passive.

examples.text: The work has been finished.
The road is being repaired.
The results will be announced tomorrow.
The form must be signed.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The road is repairing. Right: The road is being repaired.

sections.title: Using the passive
sections.intro: The passive is common when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, especially in formal and scientific writing.

rules.title: When to use the passive, and the by-agent
rules.explanation: Use the passive when the doer is unknown, obvious or less important than the action. Include by + agent only when the doer is important or adds useful information.

examples.text: My wallet has been stolen.
The suspect was arrested yesterday.
The novel was written by George Orwell.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The song was written from Lennon. Right: The song was written by Lennon.

rules.title: Get-passive and common mistakes
rules.explanation: The get-passive is informal and often describes something unexpected or negative. Some verbs, such as happen, arrive and die, are intransitive and have no passive.

examples.text: He got fired last week.
My phone got stolen.
They got married in June.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The accident was happened yesterday. Right: The accident happened yesterday.

rows: The book was written by Orwell.

groups.title: Reported speech
groups.summary: How to report statements, questions and commands, with tense, time and pronoun changes.

sections.title: Reported statements
sections.intro: Reported speech tells someone what another person said. When the reporting verb is past, the reported verb usually moves one step back.

rules.title: Say, tell and tense backshift
rules.pattern: say (that) ...; tell somebody (that) ...; past reporting verb + backshift
rules.explanation: Say does not need a person object; tell needs one. When the reporting verb is in the past, the reported verb usually moves one step back: present to past, past to past perfect, will to would.

examples.text: She said that she was tired.
She told me that she was tired.
Direct: I saw him. -> She said she had seen him.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She told that she was tired. Right: She told me that she was tired.

rules.title: When not to backshift
rules.explanation: Do not backshift when the situation is still true, when the reporting verb is in the present, or when you report a general truth. Backshift is optional when the original statement is still relevant.

examples.text: She says she is busy.
He said that water boils at 100 degrees.
She said she lives in London.

rules.mistake: Wrong: He said the sun rose in the east. Right: He said the sun rises in the east.

sections.title: Reported questions and commands
sections.intro: Reported questions use statement word order. Reported commands use an object and a to-infinitive.

rules.title: Reported questions
rules.pattern: ask + if/whether + subject + verb; ask + wh-word + subject + verb
rules.explanation: In reported questions, use statement word order: no auxiliary inversion and no question mark. Use if or whether for yes/no questions.

examples.text: Direct: Are you ready? -> She asked if I was ready.
Direct: Where do you live? -> She asked where I lived.
Direct: What time is it? -> He asked what time it was.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She asked where did I live. Right: She asked where I lived.

rules.title: Reported commands and requests
rules.explanation: Use tell for orders and ask for requests, followed by an object and a to-infinitive. Use not to for negative commands.

examples.text: Direct: Sit down. -> She told me to sit down.
Direct: Please help me. -> He asked me to help him.
Direct: Do not touch it. -> She told us not to touch it.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She said me to wait. Right: She told me to wait.

sections.title: Time, place and reporting verbs
sections.intro: Time and place words often change in reported speech. Reporting verbs also have their own grammar patterns.

rules.title: Time and place changes
rules.pattern: here -> there; now -> then; today -> that day; tomorrow -> the next day; yesterday -> the day before
rules.explanation: When you report speech later or in a different place, time and place words often change. The changes depend on the situation.

examples.text: Direct: I will do it tomorrow. -> She said she would do it the next day.
Direct: I live here. -> He said he lived there.
Direct: I saw her yesterday. -> He said he had seen her the day before.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She said she would do it tomorrow. (reported a week later) Right: She said she would do it the next day.

rules.title: Reporting verbs
rules.explanation: Different reporting verbs take different patterns. Learn the pattern with the verb: advise somebody to do, suggest doing, offer to do, apologise for doing and insist on doing.

examples.text: She admitted making a mistake.
He advised me to see a doctor.
They offered to help.
She suggested going by train.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She suggested to go by train. Right: She suggested going by train.

groups.title: Prepositions
groups.summary: At, on and in for time and place, plus other common prepositions and easily confused pairs.

sections.title: At, on and in: time
sections.intro: At is for points in time, on is for days and dates, and in is for longer periods. These are the most useful time prepositions.

rules.title: At for clock times and points in time
rules.pattern: at + clock time or point in time
rules.explanation: Use at for exact clock times and for points in the day or year that are treated as moments. It is also used in several fixed expressions.

examples.text: The class starts at nine.
We met at noon.
She works best at night.
I will see you at Christmas.
He is busy at the moment.

rules.mistake: Wrong: We met in noon. Right: We met at noon.

rules.title: On for days and dates
rules.pattern: on + day, date or day + part of day
rules.explanation: Use on with days of the week, dates and special days. Use on when a day is combined with a part of the day.

examples.text: The shop opens on Monday.
My birthday is on 5 May.
We are meeting on Friday morning.
They arrived on Christmas Day.

rules.mistake: Wrong: My birthday is in 5 May. Right: My birthday is on 5 May.

rules.title: In for longer periods
rules.pattern: in + month, year, season, part of day or period
rules.explanation: Use in for months, years, seasons, centuries and parts of the day. Use in with a period of time measured from now, such as in two weeks.

examples.text: The course begins in September.
He was born in 1998.
We often walk in the evening.
I will be back in ten minutes.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I will be back after ten minutes. (meaning within ten minutes from now) Right: I will be back in ten minutes.

rules.title: Time expressions without a preposition
rules.explanation: Do not use at, on or in before next, last, this, every, yesterday, today or tomorrow. These expressions already show time.

examples.text: We will meet next week.
She called yesterday.
I go running every morning.
This afternoon is fine.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I saw her on yesterday. Right: I saw her yesterday.

rows: at noon, at midnight, at night
at lunch, at breakfast, at the moment
at Christmas, at Easter, at the weekend
on 5 May, on my birthday, on New Year's Day
on Friday morning, on Monday evening
in 2024, in the 1990s, in the 19th century
in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening
in two weeks, in a few minutes
in the past, in the future, in my childhood
next, last, this, every, yesterday, today
next week, last year, this morning, every day
do not add at, on or in

sections.title: At, on and in: place
sections.intro: At treats a place as a point, on treats it as a surface or line, and in treats it as an enclosed space or area.

rules.title: At for points and small places
rules.pattern: at + point, small place or event
rules.explanation: Use at when you think of a place as a point on a map or a meeting place. It is common with buildings when you mean the activity inside, and with events.

examples.text: I will meet you at the station.
She is at home.
He is at work.
We were at a concert.
Turn left at the traffic lights.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I am in home. Right: I am at home.

rules.title: On for surfaces and lines
rules.pattern: on + surface, line or public transport
rules.explanation: Use on when something touches a surface, is attached to a line, or is used with public transport such as buses, trains and planes. Also use on for floors and sides.

examples.text: The book is on the table.
There is a picture on the wall.
She lives on the second floor.
I met him on the train.
The bank is on the left.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The book is in the table. Right: The book is on the table.

rules.title: In for enclosed spaces and areas
rules.pattern: in + container, area, city or country
rules.explanation: Use in for a space with limits around it, such as a box, room, building, city, country or area. Use in for the middle of something.

examples.text: The keys are in my bag.
She lives in London.
We waited in the car.
He is in the kitchen.
The shop is in the middle of the town.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She lives at London. Right: She lives in London.

rules.title: Place phrases and exceptions
rules.explanation: Some place phrases are fixed. Note arrive at for a building or point and arrive in for a city or country. Note on the corner for the outside corner and in the corner for the inside of a room.

examples.text: We arrived at the airport at six.
They arrived in Paris yesterday.
The cafe is on the corner.
The chair is in the corner of the room.
He is in bed with flu.

rules.mistake: Wrong: We arrived to the airport. Right: We arrived at the airport.

at the party, at the cinema
at home, at work, at school
small place seen as a point
at the village, at the airport
on the table, on the floor, on the wall
on the left, on the corner, on the coast
on the bus, on the train, on the plane
on the first floor, on the top floor
on Oxford Street, on the main road
in the box, in the room, in the car
in London, in France, in the north

in bed, in hospital, in prison

go home, live abroad, go upstairs

sections.title: Other common prepositions
sections.intro: These prepositions cover means, purpose, company, possession, direction and contrast.

rules.title: By, for, with and of
rules.explanation: By shows the agent, means or deadline. For shows purpose, duration or exchange. With shows company, a tool or a quality. Of shows possession, quantity or material.

examples.text: The letter was written by my aunt.
We travelled by train.
This knife is for cutting bread.
I went with my sister.
She cut the bread with a knife.
a cup of coffee

rules.mistake: Wrong: We travelled with train. Right: We travelled by train.

rules.title: To, from, into and onto
rules.explanation: To shows movement towards a destination, and from shows the starting point or origin. Into shows movement to the inside of something, and onto shows movement to a surface.

examples.text: We walked to the station.
She comes from Spain.
She walked into the room.
The cat jumped onto the table.
I gave the book to Tom.

rules.mistake: Wrong: We arrived to the station. Right: We arrived at the station.

rules.title: During, while, until and since
rules.pattern: during + noun; while + clause; until + end point; since + starting point
rules.explanation: During is a preposition and is followed by a noun. While is a conjunction and is followed by a subject and verb. Until means up to a point in time; since means from a point in the past until now.

examples.text: During the film, my phone rang.
While we were watching the film, my phone rang.
I waited until six.
I have lived here since 2015.

rules.mistake: Wrong: During I was cooking, the phone rang. Right: While I was cooking, the phone rang.

rules.title: Between, among, beside, besides, above, over, below and under
rules.pattern: between/among + noun; beside/besides + noun; above/over/below/under + noun
rules.explanation: Between is usual with two separate items; among suggests being inside a group. Beside means next to; besides means as well as or apart from. Above and over mean higher than; below and under mean lower than.

examples.text: She sat between Tom and Anna.
The house is among the trees.
Sit beside me.
Besides English, she speaks French.
The plane flew over the city.
The cat is under the chair.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Besides me, there was a chair. (meaning next to) Right: Beside me, there was a chair.

rows: during the film; while we watched
above the door; over the bridge

groups.title: Sentences and clauses
groups.summary: Clause types, relative and noun clauses, linking words, comparison, participles and emphasis.

sections.title: Clauses and sentence types
sections.intro: A clause contains a subject and a verb. Clauses can be joined by coordination or subordination.

rules.title: Clauses and sentence types
rules.explanation: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence; a dependent clause cannot. A simple sentence has one independent clause, a compound sentence has two or more, and a complex sentence has a main clause and at least one dependent clause.

examples.text: She smiled.
She smiled, and I laughed.
When the rain stopped, we went out.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Because I was tired. (as a complete sentence) Right: I went to bed because I was tired.

rules.title: Coordination and subordination
rules.pattern: independent + and/but/or/so + independent; main clause + subordinating conjunction + dependent clause
rules.explanation: Coordination joins clauses of equal importance. Subordination joins a dependent clause to a main clause. The dependent clause can come first, often followed by a comma, or after the main clause.

examples.text: I wanted to go, but I was too tired.
Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
I will call you when I arrive.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Although it was raining, but we went out. Right: Although it was raining, we went out.

sections.title: Relative, noun and adverb clauses
sections.intro: Relative clauses describe a noun. Noun clauses work like nouns. Adverb clauses show time, reason, condition or result.

rules.title: Relative clauses
rules.explanation: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing you mean and takes no commas. A non-defining relative clause adds extra information, takes commas and does not use that.

examples.text: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
The book which I bought is excellent.
My brother, who lives in Rome, is visiting.
This is the house that Jack built.

rules.mistake: Wrong: My brother, that lives in Rome, is visiting. Right: My brother, who lives in Rome, is visiting.

rules.title: Noun clauses
rules.explanation: A noun clause works like a noun: it can be the subject, object or complement of a verb. Use if or whether for yes/no ideas, and a wh-word for open questions.

examples.text: I know that she is right.
Whether he comes is still unclear.
She asked if I was ready.
What he said surprised me.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I don't know what is his name. Right: I don't know what his name is.

rules.title: Adverb clauses
rules.explanation: Adverb clauses show time, reason, condition, concession, purpose or result. They can come before or after the main clause.

examples.text: When the bell rang, we left.
I stayed because I was tired.
Although she was late, she apologised.
He studied hard so that he could pass.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Because it was raining, so we stayed inside. Right: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.

rows: people or things in defining clauses

sections.title: Linking words and comparison
sections.intro: Linking words connect ideas. Comparatives and superlatives compare people and things.

rules.title: Linking words
rules.explanation: Linking words show addition, contrast, cause, result, example or sequence. However and therefore usually start a new sentence or follow a semicolon; because and although join clauses inside one sentence.

examples.text: She was tired; however, she finished the work.
It was raining. Therefore, we stayed inside.
In addition, the service is free.
For example, many students work part-time.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She was tired, however she finished. Right: She was tired; however, she finished.

rules.title: Comparatives and superlatives
rules.pattern: adjective + -er / more + adjective + than; the + adjective + -est / the most + adjective
rules.explanation: Use the comparative to compare two things and the superlative to compare three or more. Short adjectives take -er and -est; longer adjectives take more and most. Use as ... as for equality.

examples.text: She is taller than me.
This is the most expensive restaurant in town.
He is as tall as his father.
This test is not as difficult as the last one.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She is more taller than me. Right: She is taller than me.

rows: He is as tall as me.
It is not as big as the other.
It is less expensive than that one.

sections.title: Participles, inversion and emphasis
sections.intro: Participle clauses make writing more concise. Inversion and cleft sentences move information into focus.

rules.title: Participle clauses
rules.explanation: A participle clause uses an -ing or -ed form instead of a full clause. It can show reason, time, result or condition. The subject of the participle clause should normally be the same as the subject of the main clause.

examples.text: Walking home, I saw an old friend.
Written in 1920, the novel is still popular.
Having finished the report, she went home.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Walking home, the rain started. Right: Walking home, I got caught in the rain.

rules.title: Inversion and emphasis
rules.explanation: After a negative or limiting adverbial at the beginning of a sentence, invert the subject and auxiliary. Cleft sentences and do-emphasis also move information into focus.

examples.text: Never have I seen such a mess.
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
It was Tom who called.
I do like your new coat.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Never I have seen such a mess. Right: Never have I seen such a mess.

groups.title: Punctuation
groups.summary: Full stops, commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, hyphens, dashes, quotation marks and capital letters.

sections.title: End punctuation and commas
sections.intro: End marks show where a sentence stops. Commas separate items and make the structure clearer.

rules.title: Full stops, question marks and exclamation marks
rules.explanation: Use a full stop at the end of a statement, a command or an indirect question. Use a question mark after a direct question and an exclamation mark after a strong exclamation or warning.

examples.text: She lives in Bristol.
Are you ready?
What a beautiful day!
He asked where I was going.

rules.mistake: Wrong: He asked me what time it was? Right: He asked me what time it was.

rules.title: Commas
rules.pattern: item, item and item; introductory phrase, + main clause
rules.explanation: Use commas to separate items in a list and after an introductory word or phrase. Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction that joins two independent clauses, and around non-defining relative clauses.

examples.text: We bought bread, milk and eggs.
After lunch, we went for a walk.
She was tired, so she went to bed.
My sister, who lives in Rome, is visiting.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The book, that I bought, is good. Right: The book that I bought is good.

rows: She was tired, so she left.

sections.title: Semicolons, colons and apostrophes
sections.intro: Semicolons join related clauses, colons introduce information, and apostrophes show possession or contraction.

rules.title: Semicolons and colons
rules.pattern: clause; clause; clause: list or explanation
rules.explanation: Use a semicolon to join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction. Use a colon to introduce a list, an explanation or a quotation; the part before the colon should be a complete sentence.

examples.text: I have a meeting; I will call you later.
You need three things: a pen, paper and patience.
There was one problem: the door was locked.
She said: 'I will be there.'

rules.mistake: Wrong: You need: a pen, paper and patience. Right: You need three things: a pen, paper and patience.

rules.title: Apostrophes
rules.pattern: possession: noun + 's or '; contraction: it's = it is or it has
rules.explanation: Add 's to a singular noun or an irregular plural, and only an apostrophe to a regular plural ending in -s. Its without an apostrophe is possessive; it's with an apostrophe means it is or it has.

examples.text: the girl's bag
the girls' bags
The dog wagged its tail.
It's raining.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The cat licked it's paw. Right: The cat licked its paw.

sections.title: Hyphens, dashes, quotation marks and capitals
sections.intro: These marks join words, mark breaks, show exact words and signal proper names.

rules.title: Hyphens and dashes
rules.explanation: A hyphen joins parts of a compound word or phrase and is written without spaces. A dash marks a break in a sentence and is usually written with spaces around it.

examples.text: a well-known writer
a ten-year-old child
She was tired - very tired - but she kept going.
There is one thing I need - time.

rules.mistake: Wrong: a well known writer. (as a compound adjective) Right: a well-known writer.

rules.title: Quotation marks and capitalization
rules.pattern: quotation marks around exact words; capital letter at the start and for proper nouns
rules.explanation: Use quotation marks around a person's exact words in direct speech or around a short title. Capitalise the first word of a sentence, the pronoun I, and proper nouns such as names, places, days, months, languages and nationalities.

examples.text: She said, 'I will be late.'
The chapter is called 'The Storm'.
We met on Monday in July.
I speak Spanish and English.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I met sarah on monday. Right: I met Sarah on Monday.

groups.title: Common mistakes
groups.summary: Twelve high-value errors that learners make again and again, with corrections and explanations.

sections.title: High-value learner errors
sections.intro: Each card shows the wrong form, the correct form and the reason. Learning these patterns prevents many small errors at once.

rules.title: I am agree
rules.explanation: Agree is a verb, so it does not need am, is or are. Use agree with a person or agree to a plan.

examples.text: I agree with you.
She agreed to the plan.
We all agree that the idea is good.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I am agree with you. Right: I agree with you.

rules.title: Discuss about
rules.explanation: Discuss is transitive and takes a direct object. Do not use about after discuss; use talk about if you need about.

examples.text: We discussed the problem.
They discussed the budget for an hour.
Let's talk about the problem.

rules.mistake: Wrong: We discussed about the problem. Right: We discussed the problem.

rules.title: Depend of
rules.explanation: Depend is followed by on or upon, not of. The same pattern appears in dependent on and independent of.

examples.text: It depends on the weather.
She depends on her car.
The result is dependent on hard work.

rules.mistake: Wrong: It depends of the weather. Right: It depends on the weather.

rules.title: Since and for
rules.pattern: since + starting point; for + length of time
rules.explanation: Use since with a point in time when something started, and for with a length of time. Both are common with the present perfect.

examples.text: I have lived here since 2018.
I have lived here for six years.
She has been waiting since noon.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I have lived here for 2018. Right: I have lived here since 2018.

rules.title: Make and do
rules.pattern: make + product or result; do + activity or task
rules.explanation: Use make for creating, producing or causing something. Use do for tasks, work and general activities. There is no perfect rule, so learn common phrases.

examples.text: make a cake, make a decision, make a mistake
do homework, do the washing-up, do business
She made a good impression.

rules.mistake: Wrong: I need to do a decision. Right: I need to make a decision.

rules.title: Say and tell
rules.explanation: Say does not take a person object directly; tell needs one. Use tell somebody something or tell somebody to do something.

examples.text: She said that she was tired.
She told me that she was tired.
He told us to wait.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She told that she was tired. Right: She told me that she was tired.

rules.title: Borrow and lend
rules.pattern: borrow something from somebody; lend somebody something
rules.explanation: Borrow means take something temporarily and return it. Lend means give something temporarily. The direction is opposite.

examples.text: Can I borrow your pen?
Can you lend me your pen?
She lent him her car.

rules.mistake: Wrong: Can you borrow me your pen? Right: Can you lend me your pen?

rules.title: Affect and effect
rules.explanation: Affect is usually a verb meaning 'influence'. Effect is usually a noun meaning 'result'. A less common verb effect means 'bring about'.

examples.text: The weather affects my mood.
The effect was immediate.
The new law affected thousands of people.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The rain effected our plans. Right: The rain affected our plans.

rules.title: Its and it's
rules.pattern: its = possessive; it's = it is or it has
rules.explanation: Its shows belonging. It's is a contraction of it is or it has. They are not interchangeable. If you can replace the word with it is, use it's.

examples.text: The company changed its policy.
It's a difficult question.
It's been a long day.

rules.mistake: Wrong: The dog lost it's collar. Right: The dog lost its collar.

rules.title: Then and than
rules.explanation: Then refers to time or sequence. Than introduces the second part of a comparison, and is used with comparatives such as better, more and less.

examples.text: We ate, then we left.
She is taller than me.
If you finish, then call me.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She is taller then me. Right: She is taller than me.

rules.title: Fewer and less
rules.explanation: Use fewer with plural countable nouns and less with uncountable nouns. Less is also common with numbers and measurements.

examples.text: There are fewer cars today.
We have less time than before.
It costs less than ten pounds.

rules.mistake: Wrong: There are less students this year. Right: There are fewer students this year.

rules.title: Good and well
rules.explanation: Good describes a noun. Well describes how an action is done. Well can also mean 'healthy'.

examples.text: She is a good teacher.
She teaches well.
I feel well today.

rules.mistake: Wrong: She speaks English good. Right: She speaks English well.

present.name: Present continuous
present.use: Actions now, temporary situations and arrangements.

present.name: Present perfect
present.use: Past actions with a link to now; experiences; situations that continue.

present.name: Present perfect continuous
present.use: Actions continuing up to now, often with duration.

past.name: Past simple
past.use: Completed actions at a definite past time.

past.name: Past continuous
past.use: Actions in progress at a past time.

past.name: Past perfect
past.use: An action completed before another past action.

past.name: Past perfect continuous
past.use: An action continuing up to a past point.

future.name: Future continuous
future.use: An action in progress at a future time.

future.name: Future perfect
future.use: An action completed before a future time.

future.name: Future perfect continuous
future.use: An action continuing up to a future time.
